input.text: You've reached the Yonghe Temple — Beijing's most vibrant Tibetan Buddhist temple, still thick with incense smoke and prayer. Its story begins as a royal residence: built in 1694 for the prince who would become the Yongzheng Emperor. When he took the throne, the palace could no longer be a home — so in 1744 it was converted into a monastery of the Gelug school, the "Yellow Hat" tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. That's why it looks like a palace: golden roofs and red walls, Han Chinese and Tibetan styles fused into one. Inside, don't miss the Guinness-record giant: an eighteen-meter statue of the Maitreya Buddha, carved from a single sandalwood trunk — it took three years to transport the log to Beijing. Come early, breathe the sandalwood air, and spin a prayer wheel as you go — locals will show you how.
